label: Stop 4: The Handschoenmarkt and the old lanes to the Vrijdagmarkt

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Glove Market. I'm guessing there were gloves.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's what the name says. The Handschoenmarkt, the market for gloves, right at the foot of the church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this is a really tiny square.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Small and sheltered, right under the cathedral.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look up, and you'll see the tower from very close.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why is it called the glove market?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Because the church hung gloves outside?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I can't tell you. We only know the name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We'd rather not make up a story.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Good rule.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now. This stop is mostly a walk.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From here to the Vrijdagmarkt, the Friday Market, it's a few minutes through the old lanes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which way do we go?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With the cathedral behind you, head south and a little west.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The lanes here are narrow and cobbled, and they bend.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you lose your way, look for signs to the Plantin-Moretus Museum.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Or keep your map open.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what are we looking at as we go?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The small things. Old gables. Little shop windows.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Doorways with carved details. This is a part of town that was rebuilt over and over, so you'll see different centuries in one street.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which is why my tally still says two.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I'll give you a hint. Look at the wall plaques and the corner statues.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Some of them carry the hand.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Really?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I can't promise. But the symbol is all over the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what's the Friday Market? Is it a market on Fridays?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a market square, and the name comes from that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Vrijdagmarkt is still an open square with old buildings around it, and the Plantin-Moretus Museum stands on it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Does anything still happen on Fridays?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I can't confirm the current market days, so check locally.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the square is a good place to pause, and there's a bar on it, Marigold, at number 18, listed by a local magazine among the city's cocktail bars.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Cocktails at lunchtime. I'm tempted.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Hold on. We said we'd point you to the champagne one near the end.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. I'm being good.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now, a little thread to carry through the lanes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Remember Christophe Plantin?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The printer. Moretus's father-in-law.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. He wasn't from Antwerp.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He moved here from France around 1550, and started in the lace trade and in printing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Lace. Of all things.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1576, the same year as the Spanish Fury, the family moved into the building we're walking to.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was called De Gulden Passer, the Golden Compass.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The same year as the sack.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The same year. It's a reminder that life carried on, even in the bad years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Alright. Walk with me. Which way again?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: South and a little west, down the lanes, toward the Friday Market.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And while we walk, give me something to think about.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Think about how many hands it took to print a book in the 1500s.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every letter was set by hand, one at a time.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: There it is. Another hand.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You're counting that one?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Tally says three. Don't argue.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I won't. Pause the tour here, and press play again when you reach the open square with the museum.
